name: Combined oral contraceptive pill

card.summary: The estrogen-plus-progestin birth control pill, also prescribed for hormonal acne in women because it lowers free androgens.
card.aka: The pill, COC, OCP; acne-approved brands include Ortho Tri-Cyclen, Estrostep, Beyaz and YAZ
card.note: Prescription-only; carries a small increased venous clotting risk and has formal contraindications.

quick.overview:
Combined oral contraceptives contain an estrogen and a progestin. Besides preventing pregnancy, some are prescribed to reduce acne and excess hair growth in women, because they lower the activity of androgen hormones that drive oil production in skin [1][2].

Wikipedia reports that four combined pills are FDA-approved for moderate acne in people who have started menstruating and also want contraception, and that studies show reductions in both inflammatory and non-inflammatory facial lesions [1]. Progestin-only pills have not been shown to help acne [1].
quick.mechanism: The estrogen component appears to suppress ovarian androgen production and raises sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), which reduces free testosterone. Lower free androgens mean less sebum, a major contributor to acne [1].
quick.risks: Common effects include breakthrough bleeding, nausea, headache, breast tenderness and bloating. Venous thromboembolism risk is higher in users than non-users in absolute terms (about 60 versus 30 per 100,000 woman-years) and varies by progestin; the FDA added a warning to drospirenone pill labels in 2012. Smoking over 35, migraine with aura, and a history of clots or stroke are among the listed contraindications [1].

lead: The combined oral contraceptive pill (COC, COCP, 'the pill') is a daily hormonal medicine containing an estrogen and a progestin, taken mainly for contraception. People use it for their appearance because it lowers androgen activity: less androgen-driven oil production can mean clearer skin, and the same effect is used to reduce unwanted facial and body hair [1][2][3]. It is a prescription medicine used by women, and its looks-related role is chiefly in hormonal acne, hirsutism and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

Four combined pills are FDA-approved for moderate acne in patients at least 14 or 15 years old who have begun menstruating and also want contraception: Ortho Tri-Cyclen, Estrostep, Beyaz and YAZ [1]. Studies cited by Wikipedia report roughly 40 to 70 percent fewer acne lesions with combined pills, and a 2014 review found oral antibiotics somewhat better at three months but about equal at six months [2]. For hirsutism, Wikipedia describes combined pills as functional antiandrogens with supporting evidence, some containing progestins with their own antiandrogenic activity such as cyproterone acetate, drospirenone or dienogest [3].

In PCOS, where raised androgens produce acne, hirsutism and irregular cycles, the pill is one of the standard medical options alongside metformin and lifestyle measures [4][5]. Outside dermatology the pill is discussed online mainly in debates over its effects on mood, desire and attraction, a topic on which Wikipedia's hormonal-contraception article describes the evidence as inconsistent [8][13][14].

chain: Estrogen suppresses ovarian androgen production and raises SHBG
Less free testosterone reaches oil glands and hair follicles
Less sebum and fewer acne lesions; reduced androgen-driven hair growth
angle.text: Women with hormonal acne or androgen-related hair growth use the pill to bring free androgens down, which can lead to clearer skin and finer or less facial and body hair. Wikipedia notes acne medications generally take about 8 to 12 weeks to show improvement, so effects build over months rather than days [2].

Prescription-only in many countries; on the WHO Essential Medicines list [1]
One of several standard medical options, alongside metformin [4][5]

paras: Combined pills are prescribed for androgen-related acne and hirsutism [1][3]. Wikipedia reports that third- or fourth-generation progestins (such as desogestrel, dienogest, drospirenone and norgestimate), or pills with antiandrogenic cyproterone acetate or chlormadinone acetate, are preferred for acne, and that first-generation progestins such as norethindrone and norgestrel have androgenic effects and may worsen it [2]. Progestin-only pills have not been shown to help acne [1].

For hirsutism, Wikipedia states that current data do not favour any one type of oral contraceptive over another, that insulin sensitisers are less effective than both antiandrogens and pills, and that antiandrogens are the most effective pharmacologic treatment for hirsutism that bothers the patient [3]. Because antiandrogens can harm a pregnancy, they are not recommended for people who are pregnant or planning pregnancy, which is one reason pills are used alongside or instead of them [3][2].

The primary use is pregnancy prevention, and Wikipedia lists menstrual suppression, endometriosis pain, heavy bleeding, menstrual migraine and PCOS among other uses [1]. In PCOS, international guidance reviewed in a 2022 Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology seminar lists the pill for menstrual-cycle regulation and androgen excess, with metformin used for insulin resistance and metabolic features [4]. Reviews of endometriosis and PCOS drug management cover the pill alongside other options [15][11]. A registered Phase 4 study of YAZ in China enrolled 1,921 women with contraception as the condition studied [6].

Wikipedia describes estrogens in pills as ethinylestradiol, estradiol or estetrol and progestins ranging from older norethisterone to newer drospirenone and dienogest, grouped loosely into generations whose definitions vary between sources [1][10]. Pills can be monophasic or multiphasic and come in 21-, 28- or 91-tablet packs, with some 28-day packs using a 24 active and 4 placebo split [1].

Placebo pills keep the daily routine and produce a withdrawal bleed that resembles a period. Wikipedia says monophasic pills can often be taken continuously to skip it without increasing pregnancy risk, though breakthrough bleeding may occur, and mentions extended products such as the three-month Seasonale [1]. Starting within the first five days of menstruation gives immediate contraception, while otherwise a backup method is needed for the first seven days [1].

Studies cited by Wikipedia show combined pills reduce both inflammatory and non-inflammatory facial acne lesions, whereas progestin-only pills have not shown benefit [1]. Wikipedia gives a range of about 40 to 70 percent fewer lesions and describes pills as a reasonable first-line option for some women because six-month results are comparable to antibiotics without adding antibiotic resistance [2].

Spironolactone is the other hormonal option. Wikipedia reports 33 to 85 percent fewer lesions in adult women, alone or with a pill, notes it is not FDA-approved for acne and is generally impractical for male acne because of side effects such as gynecomastia [2].

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 36 randomised trials in women with PCOS found no difference in hirsutism between metformin and the pill, or between the pill and the pill combined with metformin. The pill raised SHBG and lowered free androgen index and testosterone more than metformin did [5].

Breakthrough bleeding is the most common effect. Nausea, vomiting, headache, bloating, breast tenderness and fluid retention may also occur [1]. Wikipedia states there is no proven effect on weight [1].

The absolute risk of venous thrombosis is reported as about 60 per 100,000 woman-years in current users versus about 30 in non-users, compared with 100 to 200 per 100,000 pregnant women per year [1]. Risk is highest in the first year and varies by progestin; compared with levonorgestrel, rate ratios for deep venous thrombosis are reported as 1.82 for desogestrel, 1.86 for gestodene, 1.64 for drospirenone and 1.88 for cyproterone acetate [1]. An FDA review of more than 800,000 women led to a 2012 warning on drospirenone labels [1]. Pills with more than 50 micrograms of estrogen are linked to higher ischemic stroke and heart attack risk, and a 2015 meta-analysis found roughly 7.6-fold higher cerebral venous sinus thrombosis risk [1].

On cancer, Wikipedia reports that ovarian and endometrial cancer risk falls, while breast, cervical and liver cancer risks may rise [1]. The hormonal contraception article says the excess breast cancer risk during use fades over about ten years after stopping [8]. For mood, that article describes evidence of harm to emotional wellbeing as inconsistent, with some studies suggesting small effects in sensitive individuals and methodological problems limiting interpretation [8].

WHO and CDC eligibility criteria list as category 4 (should not be used) conditions such as migraine with aura, a history of DVT, pulmonary embolism or stroke, ischemic heart disease, smoking 15 or more cigarettes daily at age 35 or older, blood pressure of 160/100 mm Hg or higher, known thrombogenic mutations, current breast cancer and severe cirrhosis or liver tumours; pills should not be taken during known pregnancy [1]. Wikipedia notes interactions with rifampicin, St John's wort and some anticonvulsants, and that vomiting or diarrhoea can reduce absorption [1].

For contraception, progestogen negative feedback reduces pulsatile GnRH release, lowering FSH and LH, stopping follicle development and blocking the mid-cycle LH surge; the pill also thickens cervical mucus [1].

For acne and hirsutism, the estrogen component appears to suppress ovarian androgen production and raise SHBG, lowering free testosterone and therefore sebum output [1]. Some progestins add direct antiandrogen activity by blocking androgen receptors [3].

Wikipedia's account of Gregory Pincus describes a small 1951 Planned Parenthood grant, his work with M. C. Chang confirming that progesterone inhibits ovulation, and John Rock's first human trials in Brookline, Massachusetts, from 1953 [9]. Philanthropist Katharine McCormick, introduced to the research by Margaret Sanger, increased funding about fiftyfold after meeting Pincus in 1953 [9]. Large trials began in Puerto Rico in 1956, supervised by Edris Rice-Wray and Celso-Ramon Garcia, and Rice-Wray reported side effects she considered too problematic, a view Pincus and Rock disputed [9].

Wikipedia's hormonal contraception article says Enovid, the first combined pill, was approved in the US in 1957 for menstrual disorders and in 1960 as a contraceptive [8]; the FDA extended its approved uses to contraception in May 1960 [9]. First-generation pills used high estrogen doses; later generations lowered estrogen and varied the progestin, with third and fourth generations arriving from the 1990s [1].

Wikipedia states combined oral contraceptives are on the WHO List of Essential Medicines and that more than 100 million women use the pill worldwide [1]. It is prescription-only in many countries. Acne-specific approvals in the US apply to the four named pills [1].

Forum discussion of the pill is mostly outside skin care. Hacker News has carried threads on author Sarah E. Hill's argument that the pill's influence on women's brains is under-studied, a thread titled 'Study: The Pill Causes Women to Like Different Men', and a thread on whether women on the pill need simulated periods [7][13][14]. A 2019 BMJ editorial titled 'The pill and women's sexuality' addresses the sexuality question in the medical literature [12]. Posts making claims about personality, attraction and partner choice are outside the scope of acne treatment and are not established by the clinical literature cited here [8].

Human studies cited by reference sources report reductions in acne lesions with combined pills, and a 2014 review compared them with oral antibiotics [1][2]. A 2024 meta-analysis of 36 randomised trials compared the pill, metformin and both together in PCOS across hirsutism, hormone and metabolic outcomes [5]. Randomised trials have also compared dienogest with combined pills and long-acting progestogens with the pill for endometriosis pain [15]. A completed Phase 4 safety and efficacy study of YAZ in 1,921 Chinese women is registered [6].

timeline.event: Gregory Pincus begins hormonal contraceptive research with a small Planned Parenthood grant [9].
John Rock begins human trials with progesterone, and Katharine McCormick sharply increases funding [9].
Large contraceptive trials begin in Puerto Rico [9].
Enovid is approved in the US for menstrual disorders [8].
The FDA extends Enovid's approved uses to contraception [9][1].
Third- and fourth-generation progestins arrive, with lower estrogen doses than first-generation pills [1].
The FDA adds a clotting-risk warning to drospirenone pill labels [1].
A review finds oral antibiotics somewhat better than pills at three months for acne and about equal at six [2].
A meta-analysis reports about 7.6-fold higher cerebral venous sinus thrombosis risk in users [1].
A meta-analysis of 36 randomised trials compares the pill and metformin in PCOS, informing the 2023 international PCOS guideline update [5].

lore.intro: The pill rarely appears in appearance forums as a skin treatment; it is mostly debated in threads about hormones, attraction and mood, and on Hacker News as a research question [7][13][14].

claims.believers: Dermatology patients and clinicians describe it as an option when acne tracks with the cycle or androgens, and four pills carry US acne approvals [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports 40 to 70 percent fewer lesions, similar to antibiotics at six months, with improvement generally appearing over 8 to 12 weeks, and progestin choice mattering [2].

claims.claim: The pill reduces unwanted facial and body hair
claims.believers: It is described as a functional antiandrogen that lowers free testosterone [3].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says pills have supporting evidence for hirsutism and no type is favoured; antiandrogens are described as most effective, and a 2024 meta-analysis found no hirsutism difference between pill and metformin in PCOS [3][5].

claims.claim: The pill changes personality and attraction
claims.believers: A Hacker News thread discusses author Sarah E. Hill's argument that the pill's influence on women's brains is under-studied, and another is titled 'Study: The Pill Causes Women to Like Different Men' [7][13].
claims.experts: Wikipedia's hormonal contraception article says evidence of harm to emotional wellbeing is inconsistent, with small effects in sensitive individuals possible and methodological problems limiting the findings [8].

claims.claim: Women on the pill 'need' a monthly bleed
claims.believers: A Hacker News thread asks whether women on the pill need simulated periods [14].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says placebo pills produce a withdrawal bleed that resembles a period, that monophasic pills can often be taken continuously to skip it, and that this does not increase pregnancy risk [1].

claims.believers: Weight change is commonly listed as a possible side effect in reference sources [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia states there is no proven effect of the pill on weight, while listing fluid retention as a possible effect [1].

claims.claim: The pill carries no meaningful health risk
claims.believers: The pill's long record and more than 100 million users are cited as evidence of routine use [1].
claims.experts: Venous thrombosis risk is about 60 versus 30 per 100,000 woman-years, varies by progestin, and the FDA added a drospirenone warning in 2012; contraindications include migraine with aura and smoking over 35 [1].
